subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Look around wherever you are sitting right now. If you are near a torch, a mobile phone, a radio, or a solar lamp charging by the window, you are surrounded by electricity quietly doing useful work. When Amina in Hargeisa switches on an LED lamp to finish her homework after Maghrib, or when Yusuf's family in a village near the Jubba River charges phones from a small solar panel and a battery, they are all relying on one big idea: electricity can only travel through certain materials, and it is stopped by others. In this unit you will learn exactly which materials let electricity flow, which ones block it, and most importantly, how this knowledge keeps you safe.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Investigate how some materials are better conductors of electricity than others
Investigate how some metals are good conductors of electricity while most other materials are not
Know why metals are used for cables and wires and why plastics are used to cover wires and as covers for plugs and switches
Predict and test the effects of making changes to circuits, including length or thickness of wire and the number and type of components

outcomes: Explain the difference between an electrical conductor and an insulator, using the idea of moving electrons.
Test everyday household objects to find out whether they are conductors or insulators.
Describe how a simple circuit works and why it must be a complete, unbroken loop.
Draw and read simple circuit diagrams using the correct symbols for a cell, bulb, wire, and switch.
Predict what happens to a bulb when you add more cells or more bulbs to a circuit.
Explain, using science, why metal tools conduct electricity and why plastic or rubber handles keep you safe.
Apply electrical safety rules at home, especially the rule of never touching electricity with wet hands and never using mains electricity for experiments.
Study this table carefully. These are the words scientists use when they talk about electricity. You will meet them again and again, so learning them now will make everything easier.
A material that lets electric current flow through it easily.
Copper wire, aluminium foil, a steel spoon, salty water.

concepts.title: What Is Electricity Made Of?
concepts.explanation:
To understand conductors and insulators, you first need to picture what is happening inside a material — far too small to see with your eyes. Everything around you, the wire, the wood, the water, your own hand, is made of tiny building blocks called atoms. Atoms are so small that millions of them would fit across the width of a single hair. Inside each atom there is a centre, and around that centre move even tinier particles called electrons. Electrons carry a negative electrical charge.

Here is the key idea. In some materials, especially metals, a few electrons are not held tightly. They are free to drift and move from atom to atom. Scientists call these free electrons, and they sometimes picture them as a 'sea of electrons' washing through the metal. When you connect a battery, these free electrons all begin to flow in the same direction, like water pushed along a channel. That flow is what we call electric current.

In other materials, such as plastic, rubber, glass and dry wood, the electrons are held very tightly to their atoms. They cannot leave and wander about. Imagine children who must stay in their assigned seats and are not allowed to move around the room. Because these electrons cannot move freely, current cannot flow. That is why these materials are insulators.

Did You Know? Electrons in a wire actually drift very slowly, slower than an ant walking. But the electrical signal that makes them all start moving travels almost as fast as light. That is why a lamp comes on the instant you flick the switch, even though each electron barely moves.
concepts.example: It helps to hold on to one clear picture. Imagine a long pipe already completely full of water. The moment you push a little water in at one end, water immediately pours out of the far end, even though the water you pushed in has barely moved. A wire is like that pipe, already full of electrons. When the battery gives a push at one end, electrons all along the wire nudge forward together, and the effect appears at the bulb straight away. This is why you never have to wait for electricity to 'arrive' when you switch on a light. Understanding this picture will help you make sense of everything else in the unit, so take a moment to draw it or explain it aloud before you continue.

concepts.title: Conductors vs Insulators
concepts.explanation:
Now that you know the secret is moving electrons, you can understand the two great families of materials. A conductor is any material that has free electrons and therefore lets current flow through it easily. Most metals are excellent conductors: copper, aluminium, iron, steel, gold and silver. This is why the wires that carry electricity are made of metal, usually copper, because copper conducts extremely well and is not too expensive.

An insulator is a material whose electrons are locked in place, so current cannot pass. Plastic, rubber, glass, dry wood, dry paper, dry cloth and air are all good insulators. Look closely at any electric wire in your home. You will see a shiny metal core (the conductor) wrapped in a soft plastic or rubber coating (the insulator). The metal carries the electricity where we want it to go; the plastic keeps it from escaping into our fingers. This clever partnership of a conductor and an insulator working together is one of the most important ideas in the whole unit.

Some materials are surprising. Graphite, the grey 'lead' inside a pencil, is not a metal, yet it conducts electricity because its carbon atoms are arranged so that some electrons can move. Water is even more interesting: perfectly pure water is actually a poor conductor, but the ordinary water we drink, wash with, or find in a well contains dissolved minerals and salts. These dissolved substances break into charged particles called ions, and ions can carry current. This is why salty water conducts electricity well — a fact that matters enormously for safety, as you will see.

Electrons are tightly bound; none are free.

Used to coat wires because it blocks current.

Non-metal, but carbon lets some electrons move.

Why does it matter so much that some materials conduct and others do not? Because we need both. If everything conducted, electricity would leak out of every wire the moment we touched it, and nothing could be controlled or kept safe. If nothing conducted, electricity could not travel anywhere and would be useless. The whole of electrical technology, from the smallest torch to the largest power station, depends on carefully placing conductors where we want electricity to go and insulators where we want to keep it out. Every time you use an electrical device, engineers have already decided, using the science you are learning, exactly which parts should conduct and which should insulate.
concepts.example: You can also arrange conductors in an order of how well they conduct. Silver is the very best everyday conductor, followed closely by copper, then gold, then aluminium, then iron and steel. Silver and gold are far too expensive to use for ordinary wiring, so copper is the sensible choice: it conducts almost as well as silver but costs much less, and it can be pulled into long thin wires without snapping. Aluminium is lighter and cheaper still, so it is often used for the long overhead cables that carry electricity across the countryside. Choosing the right conductor is a balance of how well it conducts, how much it costs, and how easy it is to shape.

concepts.title: How a Circuit Works
concepts.explanation:
Electricity is only useful when it flows in a complete loop. This loop is called a circuit. Think of the water channels farmers dig to bring water from the Jubba or Shabelle rivers to their crops. If the channel is complete, water flows and the plants drink. If someone digs across it and breaks it, the water stops. A circuit is exactly like that, but for electricity.

A simple circuit needs three things: a source to push the current (a cell or battery), a path for the current to travel along (conducting wires), and something to use the energy, called a load (such as a bulb or a small motor). The current leaves one end of the cell, travels through the wire, passes through the bulb where it does its useful work of making light, and returns to the other end of the cell. As long as the loop is unbroken, the bulb stays lit.

If there is a break anywhere in the loop — a loose wire, a gap, or an insulator placed in the path — the current cannot flow and the bulb goes dark. This is the whole idea behind a switch. A switch is simply a controlled break in the circuit. When you push the switch 'on', two pieces of metal touch and complete the loop, so current flows. When you push it 'off', the metal pieces separate, leaving a gap, and the current stops. Every light switch in your home works this way.

[*] Remember! A circuit must be a COMPLETE, unbroken loop for current to flow. A break anywhere stops the current everywhere in a simple loop. A switch is just a break you can open and close on purpose.
concepts.example: Let us follow the journey of the current one more time, slowly, because it is the heart of this whole unit. The current begins at the negative end of the cell. It is pushed out along the wire, which is a conductor, so it travels easily. It reaches the bulb, where the wire inside is thin and the electrons have to squeeze through. As they do, they give up energy, and that energy appears as light and warmth — this is the useful work the bulb does. The current then continues along the wire and returns to the positive end of the cell, ready to be pushed round again. Round and round it goes, as long as the loop stays complete and the cell still has energy stored inside it. When the cell finally runs out of chemical energy, the push stops and the bulb goes dark. This is why torch batteries eventually go flat and must be replaced or recharged.

concepts.title: Series Circuits and Changing the Current
concepts.explanation:
When you join parts one after another in a single loop, so the current has only one path to follow, you have built a series circuit. In a series circuit, the same current flows through every part, one after the other, like a line of people passing water buckets from hand to hand along a single line. If any one person leaves the line, the whole chain stops.

You can change how brightly a bulb shines by changing the circuit. Here are the two most important rules, which you will test yourself with real batteries:

Adding more cells makes the bulb brighter. Each 1.5 V cell adds more electrical push (voltage). Two cells in series give about 3 V, which pushes the current harder, so the bulb glows more brightly. This is exactly why a large torch that takes two or three batteries shines brighter than a small torch that takes only one. Be careful though — too many cells will push so hard that the thin wire inside the bulb overheats and burns out, and the bulb 'blows'.

Adding more bulbs in series makes each bulb dimmer. When bulbs are joined one after another in the same single loop, they must share the same push from the battery. Two bulbs in series each get only half the share, so each one is dimmer than a single bulb would be. Also, because it is one single loop, if one bulb breaks or is unscrewed, the loop is broken and both bulbs go out. You may have seen old decorative string lights where the whole string goes dark when just one tiny bulb fails — that is a series circuit.
concepts.example: Did You Know? The word 'battery' really means a group of cells working together, just as a battery of drums means several drums. A single unit is really called a cell. In everyday speech people call one small cell a 'battery' too, and that is fine.

concepts.title: Circuit Symbols and Diagrams
concepts.explanation:
Scientists all over the world, from Mogadishu to Malaysia, need a quick way to draw circuits that everyone understands. Drawing a realistic picture of every wire and bulb would take too long, so instead we use simple agreed symbols. A circuit diagram is like a map: it does not look exactly like the real thing, but it shows clearly how everything is connected.

Here are the symbols you must learn to recognise and draw. Because we cannot print pictures here, each one is carefully described in words so you can draw it in your notebook:

Cell: one long thin line and one short thick line side by side. The long line is the positive (+) end, the short thick line is the negative (-) end.

Battery: two or more cell symbols drawn in a row (two long-and-short pairs).

Wire (conductor): a plain straight line joining the parts.

Bulb (lamp): a circle with a cross inside it (like a small letter X inside an O).

Switch: a small break in the line with a short line leaning up like a tiny gate or lever that can close the gap.

Open switch: the little lever is lifted, leaving a gap — current cannot flow.

Closed switch: the little lever is down, touching, so the loop is complete — current flows.
concepts.example: When you draw a circuit diagram, use a ruler to make straight lines and draw the whole circuit as a neat rectangle loop, with the symbols spaced along the sides. A tidy diagram is easy to read and helps you spot mistakes. Reading a diagram is a real scientific skill: an electrician or engineer anywhere in the world could look at your diagram and build exactly the circuit you imagined.

concepts.title: Why Metal Tools Conduct and Plastic Handles Protect
concepts.explanation:
Now let us connect the science to real life. Have you noticed that a good pair of pliers, a screwdriver, or a knife has a metal working part but a plastic or rubber handle? This is not just for comfort. The metal part conducts, and the plastic handle insulates. If the tool ever touched a live wire, the insulating handle would stop the electricity from travelling up into the person's hand. The handle is a deliberate safety barrier, designed using exactly the science you are learning.

The same thinking explains why the people who repair power lines wear thick rubber gloves and rubber boots. Rubber is an excellent insulator, so it blocks any electricity from flowing through the worker's body into the ground. It also explains why you must never poke a metal object such as a knife, fork, nail, or wire into a wall socket. Metal conducts beautifully, and mains electricity is powerful. A metal object in a socket would carry that dangerous electricity straight into your hand. Understanding conductors and insulators is therefore not only clever — it is life-saving.

Did You Know? Birds can sit safely on a single high power line without being hurt, because they are only touching one wire and electricity has no complete path through them to the ground. If the bird touched two wires at once, it would be a very different and dangerous story.
concepts.example: Think about the everyday tools around a Somali home. A cooking pot is metal so that heat passes into the food, but a good pot has a handle wrapped in wood or plastic so your hand is not burned — the same partnership of conductor and insulator, this time for heat rather than electricity. Metals tend to carry both heat and electricity well, while plastic, wood and rubber block both. This is a useful pattern to remember: the materials that make good electrical insulators usually make good heat insulators too, which is why the plastic handle on a tool protects you in more ways than one. Nature and good design both reward us for understanding which materials let energy through and which hold it back.

methods.title: Which Household Objects Conduct Electricity?
methods.example: To test everyday objects from around your home and sort them into conductors and insulators.
steps: Build a simple testing circuit: connect the battery to the bulb with wires, leaving two loose wire ends as testing probes.
First touch the two probes together. The bulb should light. This proves your circuit works.
Now hold one test object so it touches both probes at the same time, bridging the gap.
Watch the bulb. If it lights, the object is a conductor. If it stays dark, the object is an insulator.
Record your result, then remove the object and test the next one.

methods.title: Changing the Current with Cells and Bulbs
methods.example: To find out how the brightness of a bulb changes when you add more cells or more bulbs in series.
steps: Build a simple loop: one battery and one bulb. Note how bright it is (call this 'normal').
Add a second battery in series (line them up + to -). Observe the brightness now.
Return to one battery. Now add a second bulb in series (one after the other in the same loop). Observe both bulbs.
With two bulbs lit in series, gently unscrew or disconnect one bulb. Watch what happens to the other.
Record everything. Do not leave three batteries connected for long, as the bulb may blow.

methods.title: Build a Switch from Household Materials
methods.example: To build a working switch and show that a circuit only carries current when the loop is complete.
steps: Push two drawing pins into a piece of card, a short gap apart.
Loop one end of a paper clip around one pin so it can swing to touch the second pin.
Connect this switch into your battery-and-bulb loop, using the two pins as the switch contacts.
Swing the paper clip so it touches both pins (closed switch). Observe the bulb.
Swing it away so there is a gap (open switch). Observe again.

methods.title: Does Salty Water Conduct? (Guided, Battery-Only)
methods.example: To show that plain water conducts poorly but salty water conducts well, and to understand why this matters for safety. Safety First: Use ONLY a 1.5 V battery. NEVER bring mains electricity anywhere near water. Only the two battery-powered wire probes touch the water. Keep the battery and bulb away from the cup. Dry your hands before and after. This experiment shows exactly why wet hands and electricity are dangerous.
steps: Set up your testing circuit with two loose probe ends, as in Experiment 1.
Dip the two probes into the plain water, a small gap apart (do not let them touch). Observe the bulb — it will be dark or very dim.
Stir in a spoon of salt until it dissolves. Dip the probes again. Observe the bulb.
Add a little more salt, stir, and test again. Note any change.

workedExamples.title: Comparing Brightness
workedExamples.prompt: Let us reason through a common circuit question step by step, the way a scientist would.
workedExamples.solution:
Question: Aisha builds Circuit A with one 1.5 V cell and one bulb. Then she builds Circuit B with two 1.5 V cells (in series) and one identical bulb. In which circuit is the bulb brighter, and why?

Step 1 — Find the total push (voltage). Circuit A has one cell, so the push is 1.5 V. Circuit B has two cells in series, so we add them: 1.5 V + 1.5 V = 3 V.

Step 2 — Think about what voltage does. Voltage is the push that drives the current. More push means more current flows through the same bulb.

Step 3 — Connect current to brightness. A bulb glows more brightly when more current flows through its thin wire, because more electrical energy is turned into light and heat.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 2
workedExamples.prompt: Which material is the best electrical conductor? (a) plastic (b) rubber (c) copper (d) glass
workedExamples.solution: 1 (c) copper — copper is a metal with many free electrons, an excellent conductor used for wires.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 3
workedExamples.prompt: What makes metals good conductors? (a) they are heavy (b) they have free electrons (c) they are shiny (d) they are hard
workedExamples.solution: 2 (b) free electrons — metals have loosely held electrons that drift and carry current.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 4
workedExamples.prompt: A circuit must be a complete loop so that: (a) it looks neat (b) current can flow (c) the wire stays cool (d) the battery lasts longer
workedExamples.solution: 3 (b) current can flow — a break leaves a gap that stops the flow.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 5
workedExamples.prompt: Which of these is an insulator? (a) steel key (b) aluminium foil (c) dry wood (d) salty water
workedExamples.solution: 4 (c) dry wood — dry wood has no free electrons; the others all conduct.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 6
workedExamples.prompt: Adding a second cell in series to a single-bulb circuit will usually make the bulb: (a) dimmer (b) brighter (c) go out (d) change colour
workedExamples.solution: 5 (b) brighter — a second cell adds voltage (push), driving more current.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 7
workedExamples.prompt: Two identical bulbs joined one after another in a single loop will each be: (a) brighter than one bulb (b) the same (c) dimmer than one bulb (d) off
workedExamples.solution: 6 (c) dimmer than one bulb — two bulbs in series share the same push, so each gets less.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 8
workedExamples.prompt: The symbol of a circle with a cross inside it stands for a: (a) cell (b) switch (c) bulb (d) wire
workedExamples.solution: 7 (c) bulb — the circle-with-a-cross is the standard lamp/bulb symbol.

activities.title: Which Household Objects Conduct Electricity?
activities.materials: One 1.5 V battery (AA or similar); One small torch bulb or LED; Two or three pieces of wire (single-strand copper is easiest); A little tape to hold connections; Objects to test: metal spoon, steel key, aluminium foil, coin, plastic ruler, rubber band, dry wooden stick, dry cloth, glass marble, pencil graphite (a sharpened pencil), paper clip, plastic bottle cap
steps: Build a simple testing circuit: connect the battery to the bulb with wires, leaving two loose wire ends as testing probes.
First touch the two probes together. The bulb should light. This proves your circuit works.
Now hold one test object so it touches both probes at the same time, bridging the gap.
Watch the bulb. If it lights, the object is a conductor. If it stays dark, the object is an insulator.
Record your result, then remove the object and test the next one.

Return to one battery. Now add a second bulb in series (one after the other in the same loop). Observe both bulbs.
With two bulbs lit in series, gently unscrew or disconnect one bulb. Watch what happens to the other.
Record everything. Do not leave three batteries connected for long, as the bulb may blow.
Safety: Use only a small 1.5 V battery. Never use plug sockets or mains electricity, and disconnect the battery when you finish.

activities.title: Build a Switch from Household Materials
activities.materials: One 1.5 V battery, one bulb, wires; Two metal drawing pins or a paper clip and two pins; A small piece of card or a bottle cap as a base
steps: Push two drawing pins into a piece of card, a short gap apart.
Loop one end of a paper clip around one pin so it can swing to touch the second pin.
Connect this switch into your battery-and-bulb loop, using the two pins as the switch contacts.
Swing the paper clip so it touches both pins (closed switch). Observe the bulb.
Swing it away so there is a gap (open switch). Observe again.

Safety: Pins and nails have sharp points — ask an adult to help, and store them safely afterwards. Use only a small 1.5 V battery. Never use plug sockets or mains electricity, and disconnect the battery when you finish.

activities.title: Does Salty Water Conduct? (Guided, Battery-Only)
activities.materials: One 1.5 V battery, one bulb or LED, wires; A cup of plain water; A spoon of table salt; A dry cloth for spills
steps: Set up your testing circuit with two loose probe ends, as in Experiment 1.
Dip the two probes into the plain water, a small gap apart (do not let them touch). Observe the bulb — it will be dark or very dim.
Stir in a spoon of salt until it dissolves. Dip the probes again. Observe the bulb.
Add a little more salt, stir, and test again. Note any change.
Observation Sheet
Safety: Use only a small 1.5 V battery. Never use plug sockets or mains electricity, and disconnect the battery when you finish.

activities.materials: One 1.5 V battery (AA or similar); One small torch bulb or LED; Two or three pieces of wire (single-strand copper is easiest); A little tape to hold connections; Objects to test: metal spoon, steel key, aluminium foil, coin, plastic ruler, rubber band, dry wooden stick, dry cloth, glass marble, pencil graphite (a sharpened pencil), paper clip, plastic bottle cap
steps: Look for an example of circuit symbols and diagrams around your home or outside.
Watch it closely for a few minutes and note three things you notice.
Write or draw what you observed, using the words Part and Cell.

rules.title: What Is Electricity Made Of?
rules.text: To understand conductors and insulators, you first need to picture what is happening inside a material — far too small to see with your eyes.

rules.title: Conductors vs Insulators
rules.text: Now that you know the secret is moving electrons, you can understand the two great families of materials.

rules.title: How a Circuit Works
rules.text: Electricity is only useful when it flows in a complete loop.

rules.title: Series Circuits and Changing the Current
rules.text: When you join parts one after another in a single loop, so the current has only one path to follow, you have built a series circuit.

rules.title: Circuit Symbols and Diagrams
rules.text: Scientists all over the world, from Mogadishu to Malaysia, need a quick way to draw circuits that everyone understands.

rules.title: Why Metal Tools Conduct and Plastic Handles Protect
rules.text: Now let us connect the science to real life.

realProblems.prompt: Amina's torch is dim. She has three fresh 1.5 V batteries. What could she do to make it brighter, and what risk must she avoid?
realProblems.answer: She can add a second (or third) cell in series to raise the voltage and brighten the torch. She must avoid adding so many cells that the bulb overheats and blows, and must only ever use the small batteries — never mains.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Part, Cell, Battery — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: She can add a second (or third) cell in series to raise the voltage and brighten the torch. She must avoid adding so many cells that the bulb overheats and blows, and must only ever use the small batteries — never mains.

realProblems.prompt: Yusuf's family charges phones from a solar panel and a battery. Explain the job of the copper wires and the plastic coating on those wires.
realProblems.answer: The copper wires are conductors carrying the electricity from the battery to the phones; the plastic coating is an insulator that keeps the current inside the wire and the family safe.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Part, Cell, Battery — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: The copper wires are conductors carrying the electricity from the battery to the phones; the plastic coating is an insulator that keeps the current inside the wire and the family safe.

realProblems.prompt: After doing the dishes, Halima wants to switch on the light. What should she do first, and why?
realProblems.answer: She should dry her hands fully first, because wet skin conducts electricity much more easily, making a shock more likely.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Part, Cell, Battery — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: She should dry her hands fully first, because wet skin conducts electricity much more easily, making a shock more likely.

realProblems.prompt: Omar finds a cable in the yard with cracked plastic and bare metal showing. What should he do, and why is the bare metal dangerous?
realProblems.answer: He should not touch it and should tell a trusted adult, because the bare metal is a conductor that could carry dangerous current into anyone who touches it.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Part, Cell, Battery — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: He should not touch it and should tell a trusted adult, because the bare metal is a conductor that could carry dangerous current into anyone who touches it.

realProblems.prompt: Explain why you must never poke a metal fork into a wall socket, using the words conductor and mains electricity.
realProblems.answer: Metal is an excellent conductor, and mains electricity is very powerful (around 220 V). A fork in a socket would carry that dangerous electricity straight into your hand.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Part, Cell, Battery — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: Metal is an excellent conductor, and mains electricity is very powerful (around 220 V). A fork in a socket would carry that dangerous electricity straight into your hand.

realProblems.prompt: Two circuits both use one bulb. Circuit X has one cell; Circuit Y has two cells in series. Predict which bulb is brighter and explain each step of your reasoning.
realProblems.answer: Circuit Y is brighter. Step 1: Y has 1.5 V + 1.5 V = 3 V; X has 1.5 V. Step 2: more voltage means more push. Step 3: more push drives more current through the bulb. Step 4: more current makes it glow brighter — so Y is brighter.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Part, Cell, Battery — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: Circuit Y is brighter. Step 1: Y has 1.5 V + 1.5 V = 3 V; X has 1.5 V. Step 2: more voltage means more push. Step 3: more push drives more current through the bulb. Step 4: more current makes it glow brighter — so Y is brighter.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: In your own words, explain the difference between a conductor and an insulator.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A conductor lets electric current flow through it easily because it has free electrons (e.g. metals). An insulator does not let current flow because its electrons are tightly bound (e.g. plastic, rubber).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why must a circuit be a complete loop? What happens if there is a break?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A circuit must be a complete loop so current has an unbroken path from the cell, through the parts, and back. If there is a break, the current stops everywhere and the bulb goes dark.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain why adding more cells in series makes a bulb brighter.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Each cell adds more voltage (push). More push drives more current through the bulb, so it glows brighter. (Too many cells can blow the bulb.)

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain why adding more bulbs in series makes each bulb dimmer.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Bulbs in series must share the battery's push. With two bulbs, each gets only about half the share, so each is dimmer than a single bulb would be.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why do line workers wear rubber gloves and boots?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Rubber is a good insulator, so gloves and boots block electricity from flowing through the worker's body to the ground, preventing shock.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Give two reasons you must never touch a switch with wet hands.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Wet skin conducts far better than dry skin, and water may contain ions. Touching a switch with wet hands gives electricity an easy path through you, risking a dangerous shock.

rounds.explanation: dimmer than one bulb — two bulbs in series share the same push, so each gets less.

games.title: Spot the Error: Switch
games.description: Practise switch through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: For safe experiments you should use:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: a 1.5 V battery — small batteries are safe; mains and engines are dangerous.

rounds.prompt: Which material is the best electrical conductor?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: copper — copper is a metal with many free electrons, an excellent conductor used for wires.

rounds.prompt: Which of these is an insulator?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: dry wood — dry wood has no free electrons; the others all conduct.

rounds.prompt: The symbol of a circle with a cross inside it stands for a:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: bulb — the circle-with-a-cross is the standard lamp/bulb symbol.

games.title: Mastery Mix: Series circuit
games.description: Practise series circuit through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: A switch turns a circuit off by:
choices: making a gap in the loop
rounds.answer: making a gap in the loop
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: making a gap in the loop — opening the switch breaks the circuit.

rounds.prompt: What makes metals good conductors?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: free electrons — metals have loosely held electrons that drift and carry current.

rounds.prompt: Adding a second cell in series to a single-bulb circuit will usually make the bulb:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: brighter — a second cell adds voltage (push), driving more current.

rounds.prompt: Why is salty water dangerous with electricity but pure water much less so?
choices: salt forms ions that carry current
rounds.answer: salt forms ions that carry current
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: salt forms ions that carry current — dissolved salt makes charged ions; pure water lacks them.

games.title: Unit Champion: Ion
games.description: Practise ion through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: Which best explains why a bird can sit safely on one power line?
choices: there is no complete path through the bird to the ground
rounds.answer: there is no complete path through the bird to the ground
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: no complete path through the bird to the ground — touching only one wire means no loop.

rounds.prompt: A circuit must be a complete loop so that:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: current can flow — a break leaves a gap that stops the flow.

rounds.prompt: Two identical bulbs joined one after another in a single loop will each be:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: dimmer than one bulb — two bulbs in series share the same push, so each gets less.

rounds.prompt: Why do good tools have plastic or rubber handles?
choices: to insulate and protect the user
rounds.answer: to insulate and protect the user
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: to insulate and protect the user — the insulating handle stops current reaching the hand.

selfAssessment: I can explain the difference between an electrical conductor and an insulator, using the idea of moving electrons.
I can test everyday household objects to find out whether they are conductors or insulators.
I can describe how a simple circuit works and why it must be a complete, unbroken loop.
I can draw and read simple circuit diagrams using the correct symbols for a cell, bulb, wire, and switch.
I can predict what happens to a bulb when you add more cells or more bulbs to a circuit.
I can explain, using science, why metal tools conduct electricity and why plastic or rubber handles keep you safe.
I can apply electrical safety rules at home, especially the rule of never touching electricity with wet hands and never using mains electricity for experiments.
I can study this table carefully. These are the words scientists use when they talk about electricity. You will meet them again and again, so learning them now will make everything easier.
